memories.gist: The lock file must be committed from a clean install or transitive versions drift between machines.
memories.content: Running the install with an existing partial tree produces a lock file that pins different transitive versions than a clean install does. The drift shows up as a test passing on one machine and failing on another. Delete the tree and reinstall before committing a lock change.

memories.gist: Node builds need the heap size raised explicitly or the bundler dies late in the build with no clear message.
memories.content: The bundler exceeds the default heap on the largest entry point. It dies with an abort trace that does not name memory. Set the max-old-space option in the build script rather than in a developer's shell so CI gets it too.

memories.gist: Test ordering is randomised by default in this repo, so a suite that only passes in file order is hiding a dependency.
memories.content: The runner is configured to shuffle within a module. If a test only passes in declaration order it is depending on state left by a neighbour. Do not disable the shuffle to make it pass; fix the shared state.

memories.gist: The coverage gate measures only changed lines, so a large refactor can drop total coverage and still pass.
memories.content: The gate is diff-scoped. That is deliberate, but it means total coverage can decline while every individual change passes. Watch the trend chart, not the per-PR verdict.

memories.gist: The build requires the newer builder backend; with the legacy backend the cache mounts are silently ignored.
memories.content: Cache mount directives are a no-op on the legacy builder, so the build succeeds but takes several times longer with no warning. Export the builder selection variable in CI explicitly.

memories.gist: The partner's older endpoint still requires the deprecated TLS version, so it must be reached through the proxy.
memories.content: One partner endpoint has not moved off the deprecated protocol version, which our default client refuses. Route those calls through the compatibility proxy rather than weakening the client's minimum version globally.

memories.gist: Application logs are sampled at one in ten above a rate threshold, so a missing log line does not prove the code did not run.
memories.content: The logging pipeline samples aggressively once a service exceeds a per-second threshold. People conclude a branch never executed because its log line is absent. Use a counter metric for anything you need to reason about reliably.

memories.gist: Traces are head-sampled at one percent, so most requests have no trace and searching for a specific request usually fails.
memories.content: Head sampling at one percent means a given request almost certainly has no trace. Tail sampling was discussed and not implemented. For a specific investigation, enable the per-request debug header, which forces capture.

memories.gist: Adding a label with unbounded values to a metric will get the metric dropped by the collector's cardinality guard.
memories.content: The collector enforces a series-per-metric ceiling and drops the whole metric when exceeded, not just the new series. A metric silently disappearing from dashboards is usually this. Keep labels to bounded enumerations.

memories.gist: The latency alert flaps during deploys because the rollout briefly serves from fewer instances; it is not actionable.
memories.content: During a rolling deploy the remaining instances take extra load and p99 crosses the alert threshold for a minute or two. It self-resolves. The alert has not been given a deploy-aware inhibition rule yet, so it is routinely ignored, which is its own problem.

memories.gist: Rotating the signing key requires both keys to be trusted for one full token lifetime, or in-flight tokens are rejected.
memories.content: The verifier must accept old and new keys during the overlap, which is the token lifetime plus a margin. Cutting straight over invalidates every token issued before the switch. The rotation script does the overlap; doing it by hand usually does not.

memories.gist: The encryption key is region-pinned, so a failover to the secondary region cannot decrypt existing payloads.
memories.content: The key exists only in the primary region. A regional failover leaves the secondary unable to decrypt anything already stored. This is a known gap in the disaster-recovery story and is documented as accepted risk rather than fixed.

memories.gist: Newly granted permissions take up to a minute to become effective, so a permission test immediately after granting is unreliable.
memories.content: Policy propagation is eventually consistent. A script that grants and then immediately exercises the permission will fail intermittently. Add a retry loop around the first authorised call rather than a fixed sleep.

memories.gist: Listing the artefact bucket without a prefix walks millions of keys and costs real money; always pass a prefix.
memories.content: The artefact bucket has millions of objects. An unprefixed list is slow and billed per request page. A cleanup script that did this once produced a noticeable line item. Always scope with a prefix and a max-keys bound.

memories.gist: CDN invalidation is not instant and is billed per path, so bulk invalidation after a deploy is the wrong pattern.
memories.content: Invalidations take minutes to propagate and are charged per path above a monthly free allowance. Deploys should change the asset URL instead, which makes invalidation unnecessary. The build already emits content-hashed names for this reason.

memories.gist: The queue's visibility timeout is shorter than the worst-case handler duration, so slow messages get delivered twice.
memories.content: A handler that exceeds the visibility timeout has its message redelivered while still processing, producing duplicate side effects. Handlers must be idempotent, and the two that are not are known and tracked. Extending the timeout has knock-on effects on redrive.

memories.gist: The dead-letter queue has no alarm on it, so poison messages accumulate unnoticed.
memories.content: Messages that exhaust their receive count land in the dead-letter queue and nothing watches it. A batch of malformed events sat there for three weeks. An alarm on queue depth is the obvious fix and has not been done.

memories.gist: The idempotency key is derived from the payload hash, so a retry with a reordered map produces a different key.
memories.content: Because the key is a hash of the serialised payload and map ordering is not stable across languages, a retry from a different client can produce a different key and duplicate the effect. Sort keys before hashing; the Python client does, the other one does not.

memories.gist: Duration measurement must use the monotonic clock; the wall clock steps backwards during synchronisation and produces negative durations.
memories.content: Negative durations in the metrics come from measuring with the wall clock across a time synchronisation step. Use the monotonic clock for all interval measurement. Several older call sites still do not.

memories.gist: Forking after threads have started leaves locks held in the child, which deadlocks on the first allocation.
memories.content: The worker pool forks. If any library has already started a thread that holds an internal lock, the child inherits the locked state and hangs immediately. Start the pool before anything else, and never fork lazily on first use.

memories.gist: The graceful-shutdown handler is registered too late, so a fast rollout kills the process before it can drain.
memories.content: The termination handler is installed after the server begins accepting connections, so a signal arriving in that window is handled by the default disposition and the process dies without draining. Register the handler first.

memories.gist: The readiness and liveness probes point at the same endpoint, so a slow dependency causes restarts instead of removal from the pool.
memories.content: Both probes hit one endpoint that checks the downstream dependency. When the dependency is slow, liveness fails and the orchestrator restarts a healthy process. Split them: liveness should check only the process, readiness may check dependencies.

memories.gist: The autoscaler's scale-down window is shorter than the pod start time, so load spikes cause oscillation.
memories.content: Scale-down happens faster than new instances can become ready, so the autoscaler removes capacity it is about to need. Lengthening the stabilisation window fixed it; changing the target utilisation did not.

memories.gist: The GPU node pool is tainted, so a workload without the matching toleration schedules on CPU nodes and runs a hundred times slower.
memories.content: There is no error when the toleration is missing. The pod schedules on a general node and the workload falls back to CPU. It looks like a performance regression rather than a scheduling mistake. Assert on the device count at start.

memories.gist: Config map changes are not picked up without a restart, because the mount is read once at start.
memories.content: The process reads the mounted config at start and caches it. Editing the config map updates the file on disk within a minute but nothing rereads it. A rollout restart is required; there is no watch.

memories.gist: The init container that runs migrations will retry forever if the database is unreachable, so a bad connection string looks like a slow start.
memories.content: The migration init container has no failure ceiling and retries indefinitely, so a typo in the connection string presents as a pod stuck in initialisation with no obvious error. Check the init container logs specifically; the main container has none yet.

memories.gist: Volume expansion works online but shrinking does not, so over-provisioning is a one-way decision.
memories.content: Volumes can be grown in place without downtime. They cannot be shrunk at all; the only path is create-new-and-copy. Size conservatively at first.

memories.gist: The nightly job has no concurrency guard, so a run that overruns into the next window doubles up.
memories.content: When the nightly job takes longer than its interval, a second instance starts alongside it. The two then contend on the same rows and both slow down, which makes the overlap worse. A lease-based guard is the fix; the scheduler's own concurrency policy was not honoured in this deployment.

memories.gist: The scheduler runs in UTC, so a job specified for local business hours drifts by an hour twice a year.
memories.content: Schedules are evaluated in UTC with no zone support. A job intended for local morning runs an hour early or late after a daylight change. Either accept the drift or compute the schedule from a zone-aware generator.

memories.gist: The time library used by the report boundary does not handle the repeated second, which double-counts one row per occurrence.
memories.content: A repeated second produces two rows with identical timestamps and the boundary logic counts both into each window. It is a once-in-years event and the impact is one row, so it has been documented rather than fixed.

memories.gist: Monetary amounts are stored as integer minor units; any code that converts to float for arithmetic will produce off-by-one totals.
memories.content: Amounts are integers in minor units precisely to avoid representation error. A helper that converted to float for a percentage calculation reintroduced it and produced totals off by a unit. Do percentage maths in integers with explicit rounding.

memories.gist: The decimal context precision is set globally at import, so a library that changes it affects unrelated calculations.
memories.content: One module sets the global decimal context at import time. Anything imported after it inherits the change, which has produced surprising rounding in unrelated code. Use a local context manager instead.

memories.gist: String sorting depends on the process locale, so ordering differs between the container and a developer machine.
memories.content: Sort order for non-ASCII strings follows the locale, which is unset in the container and set on most laptops. A test asserting on order therefore passes locally and fails in CI. Sort with an explicit key rather than relying on default collation.

memories.gist: The validation regex backtracks catastrophically on a long input, which is a denial-of-service path on a public endpoint.
memories.content: One nested-quantifier pattern takes exponential time on adversarial input. On the public endpoint that is a denial-of-service. It was replaced with an explicit parser. Do not reintroduce nested quantifiers in request validation.

memories.gist: Anchors and aliases in the config are expanded by the loader but not by the schema validator, so validated config differs from loaded config.
memories.content: The validator runs on the raw document and sees the alias node; the loader expands it. A config can therefore pass validation and load differently. Avoid anchors in files that are validated.

memories.gist: Multi-line strings in the config preserve leading whitespace, which breaks the embedded query when the config is reindented.
memories.content: An embedded query is stored as a multi-line string. Reindenting the config file changes the string content and, for one query, changed its meaning. Move embedded queries to their own files.

memories.gist: Quotes in the environment file are taken literally by the runtime but stripped by the shell loader, so behaviour differs by launch path.
memories.content: Launching through the shell wrapper strips quotes; launching the binary directly with the file loaded by the runtime does not. A value with quotes therefore differs by launch path. Do not quote values in that file.

memories.gist: The build fails on the Windows runner only, because the intermediate object paths exceed the path length limit.
memories.content: Deeply nested intermediate directories exceed the platform path limit on one runner. The failure names a file that exists, which is confusing. Shorten the build output directory; long-path support was enabled and did not help for this toolchain.

memories.gist: Two files differing only in case exist in the repo, which breaks checkout on case-insensitive filesystems.
memories.content: A rename that changed only case left two paths in history. Checkout on a case-insensitive filesystem collides and reports a dirty tree immediately after clone. The tracked fix is to rename one via a two-step change.

memories.gist: A file already tracked is not affected by adding it to the ignore file, which is why the local config keeps getting committed.
memories.content: Ignore rules only apply to untracked paths. The local config was committed once, so it continues to be tracked and shows up in every diff. It needs an explicit index removal, which will delete it for everyone on next pull unless they save a copy.

memories.gist: Submodules check out a detached commit, so edits made inside one are easy to lose.
memories.content: A submodule is at a commit, not a branch. Work done inside it without first checking out a branch is on no branch and is lost on the next update. Check out a branch inside the submodule before editing.

memories.gist: Large files are stored out of band and a clone without the extension installed yields pointer files that fail at runtime with a parse error.
memories.content: Without the extension, the working tree contains small text pointer files where binaries should be. The failure is a parse error in whatever reads them, which does not suggest the real cause. Install the extension and re-fetch.

memories.gist: The CI clone is shallow, so anything that reads history further back than one commit fails only in CI.
memories.content: The default CI checkout fetches a single commit. Version derivation from tags, and any diff against the merge base, therefore fail or produce wrong answers. Ask for the deeper fetch explicitly in the job that needs it.

memories.gist: CI builds the merge result, not your branch tip, so a green branch can fail after an unrelated change lands on the target.
memories.content: The pipeline builds the merge of your branch with the current target. A failure can therefore be caused by something that landed on the target after your last push. Re-run before assuming your change is at fault.

memories.gist: The pre-push hook runs the full suite, which makes an interactive rebase with many commits take a very long time.
memories.content: The hook runs on every pushed commit rather than once per push, so a rebase that rewrites twenty commits runs the suite twenty times. There is a documented environment variable to run it once; it is not the default.

memories.gist: Release tags are protected and cannot be moved, so a bad release requires a new patch tag rather than a retag.
memories.content: Tag protection is on. A mistake in a release requires cutting the next patch version. Attempting to force-update a tag fails at the server, which is intentional and has saved us at least once.

memories.gist: The changelog is generated from commit subjects, so a squash merge with a generic subject loses the detail.
memories.content: Generation reads commit subjects on the target branch. A squash merge collapses everything into one subject, so a descriptive body is not picked up. Write the subject as the changelog line you want.

memories.gist: Dependencies in the pre-one version range are treated as breaking on every minor bump by the resolver, so ranges do not do what you expect there.
memories.content: For versions below one, the resolver treats the minor position as the breaking position. A caret range therefore does not span minor versions. Two of our dependencies are in that range and must be pinned exactly.

memories.gist: Pinning a transitive dependency requires an override entry; adding it as a direct dependency does not constrain the transitive resolution.
memories.content: Adding the package as a direct dependency at the wanted version leaves the transitive resolution free to pick another, and the loader may get either. The override mechanism is the only reliable way. This has bitten us twice.

memories.gist: One dependency has no wheel for the runtime version we use, so it compiles from source and adds several minutes to every cold install.
memories.content: The cold install compiles that package because no matching wheel is published. It is a few minutes each time and is the main reason the dependency cache matters. A prebuilt wheel is published internally now but the index priority has not been changed to prefer it.

memories.gist: The installer will silently pick an older version to satisfy a conflict rather than failing, which is how a very old library ended up installed.
memories.content: Given an unsatisfiable constraint set the resolver backtracks to an old version that does satisfy it, and reports success. A library several major versions behind was installed this way and only noticed when an expected function was missing. Read the resolved versions after any dependency change.

memories.gist: An editable install shadows the packaged version in a way that hides missing package data files until deployment.
memories.content: Under an editable install, data files are read from the source tree whether or not they are declared for packaging. Anything undeclared works in development and is missing in the built artefact. Build the artefact and test against it before release.

memories.gist: Two distributions contribute to the same namespace, and installing one without the other produces a partially populated package with confusing import errors.
memories.content: The namespace is split across two distributions. Installing only one leaves imports of the other's modules failing with an error that names the namespace, not the missing distribution. Both are required and neither declares the other.

memories.gist: Importing the client module opens a connection as a side effect, which makes it unsafe to import at module scope in the worker.
memories.content: The client module connects at import. In the forking worker that means a connection is created pre-fork and shared, which produces interleaved protocol errors. Import it inside the function, or use the lazy factory.

memories.gist: The two modules import each other and only work because one import is inside a function; moving it to the top breaks start-up.
memories.content: There is a genuine cycle, worked around by a function-scoped import. A well-intentioned tidy-up that hoisted it to the top produced an import error at start. The cycle should be broken properly but the refactor is large.

memories.gist: Handlers register themselves on import, so a handler in a module nobody imports is silently absent.
memories.content: Registration is a decorator side effect. If the module is never imported the handler does not exist and requests for it fall through to the default with no error. The package's init imports them all explicitly for this reason; add new ones there.

memories.gist: Enum values are serialised by name in one path and by ordinal in another, so reordering the enum breaks stored data.
memories.content: One serialiser writes the name, the other writes the position. Inserting a value in the middle therefore invalidates anything stored by the second. Append new values at the end only, until the ordinal path is removed.

memories.gist: The environment parser treats any non-empty string as true, so setting a flag to the string false enables it.
memories.content: There is no truthiness parsing; presence and non-emptiness are the test. Setting a flag to the literal text false turns it on, which has caught several people. Unset the variable to disable.

memories.gist: The API distinguishes an explicit null from an absent field, and the client's default serialiser omits nulls, so clearing a field is impossible through it.
memories.content: Clearing a field requires sending an explicit null. The client omits null fields by default, so a clear is indistinguishable from no change. Enable the include-nulls option on that specific call.

memories.gist: The serialisation library must stay at v1.9.4; v1.10.0 changed default field ordering and invalidates stored blobs.
memories.content: v1.10.0 changed the default field ordering in the compact encoding, so blobs written by it cannot be read by anything older and vice versa. We have stored blobs, so we are pinned at v1.9.4 until a migration exists. The incompatibility is silent: reads produce garbage values rather than errors.

memories.gist: Do not take the v3.0.0-rc line of the HTTP client; its connection pool leaks sockets under cancellation.
memories.content: The release candidate leaks a socket per cancelled request. Under a load shedder that cancels aggressively it exhausts descriptors within an hour. Stay on the v2 line until a final v3 ships.

memories.gist: The linter is pinned at v0.14.2 because v0.15 added a rule that fires on most of the codebase.
memories.content: v0.15 enabled a new rule by default that flags a pattern used widely in our code. Adopting it is a large mechanical change nobody has scheduled. Pinned at v0.14.2 with the upgrade tracked as a separate task.

memories.gist: v2.4.0 of the pipeline library reverted the retry default change, so the explicit setting is no longer required but is harmless.
memories.content: The retry default was restored in v2.4.0 after complaints. Explicitly setting retries is now redundant but does no harm and is worth keeping so the intent is visible in the code.

memories.gist: The build targets Java 11 bytecode even though the toolchain is 17, and mixing a 17-compiled dependency produces a version error at class load.
memories.content: Target level is 11 for a consumer that has not upgraded. A dependency compiled for 17 fails at class load with an unsupported class file version message that names the numeric level, not the release. Check the dependency's target before adding it.

memories.gist: One native dependency has no build for Python 3.12, which is why the venv is created with 3.11.
memories.content: The dependency's build fails on 3.12 because of a removed C API. Until it is updated the project pins 3.11 in the version file. Creating a 3.12 venv appears to work until that install step.

memories.gist: LOG_LEVEL is read only by the application logger; the access log has its own separate variable.
memories.content: Setting LOG_LEVEL to debug does not increase access-log verbosity, which has its own control. People conclude debug logging is broken. Both need setting to get a full picture.

memories.gist: HTTPS_PROXY is honoured by one HTTP client in the stack and ignored by the other, so proxied traffic is partial.
memories.content: One client reads the proxy variables from the environment, the other requires explicit configuration. In a proxied environment half the outbound traffic bypasses the proxy and is blocked. Configure the second client explicitly.

memories.gist: TMPDIR is set to a small in-memory filesystem in the container, so large temporary files fail with a disk-full error.
memories.content: The container sets TMPDIR to a memory-backed mount sized in tens of megabytes. Anything that spools a large file there fails with no space left, which is confusing because the real disk is nearly empty. Pass an explicit directory for large spooling.

memories.gist: PYTHONPATH is set in the entrypoint and shadows the installed package with a stale copy baked into the image.
memories.content: The entrypoint prepends a directory that contains an older copy of the package. Imports resolve to the stale copy, so a fix that is definitely in the installed distribution appears not to take. Remove the prepend; it exists for a dependency that no longer needs it.

memories.gist: SERVICE_TOKEN and AUTH_TOKEN are different credentials for different hops and are frequently confused.
memories.content: SERVICE_TOKEN authenticates to the internal mesh; the other authenticates to the external API. They are both opaque strings of similar length, and swapping them produces an unhelpful generic rejection. Check which hop is rejecting before assuming the credential is wrong.

memories.gist: FEATURE_FLAGS is a comma-separated allow list with no validation, so a typo silently disables a feature.
memories.content: Unrecognised entries are ignored without a warning. A misspelled flag therefore means the feature is off and nothing says so. The list of valid names is only in the source. A validating loader is an obvious improvement nobody has made.

memories.gist: AWS_REGION being unset makes the client default to a region we do not use, producing confusing not-found errors.
memories.content: With no region set the client falls back to its own default, where none of our resources exist. The resulting error says the resource does not exist, which is true in that region. Always set it explicitly, including in local scripts.

memories.gist: NO_COLOR is honoured by the test reporter but not the build tool, so CI logs are half full of escape codes.
memories.content: The reporter respects it, the build tool needs its own flag. CI logs therefore contain escape sequences from one of the two. Pass both.

memories.gist: org.example.io.JsonSerializer is not thread safe despite being registered as a singleton.
memories.content: It holds a mutable buffer as instance state and is wired as a singleton, so concurrent use corrupts output. It manifests as truncated or interleaved payloads under load. Construct one per call, or use the stateless variant.

memories.gist: org.example.metrics.Registry silently drops registrations made after the exporter has started.
memories.content: Registering a metric after the exporter's first scrape has no effect and logs nothing, so a metric added in a lazily-initialised code path never appears. Register everything eagerly at start.

memories.gist: com.legacy.transport.Client swallows interrupt, so cancellation does not propagate and shutdown hangs.
memories.content: The old transport client catches and discards the interrupt, so a cancelled call keeps running and the shutdown wait times out. Wrap calls with a timeout of your own rather than relying on cancellation.

memories.gist: org.example.core.Validator caches compiled schemas keyed by name only, so two schemas with the same name collide.
memories.content: The cache key omits the namespace, so two same-named schemas from different namespaces resolve to whichever was compiled first. Validation then passes or fails for the wrong reasons. Names are unique in practice today, which is why this has not bitten yet.

memories.gist: Settings in setup.cfg are ignored now that pyproject.toml declares the same tool section, and the shadowing is silent.
memories.content: Both files exist. For tools that read both, the newer file wins and the older section is ignored with no warning, so editing the file you find first often has no effect. Consolidate into the newer file.

memories.gist: The editor config sets tabs for one directory only, and the formatter does not read the editor config, so the two disagree.
memories.content: One legacy directory is tab-indented per the editor config. The formatter has its own configuration that does not know about that exception and reformats to spaces, producing a large diff. Exclude the directory in the formatter config too.

memories.gist: Missing entries in the ignore file send the whole working tree to the build daemon, which is why builds are slow on a dirty tree.
memories.content: The build context includes everything not excluded, so local virtual environments and caches are uploaded. On a dirty tree that is gigabytes and dominates build time. Keep the ignore file in sync with the ignore rules for version control.

memories.gist: The build file requires tab indentation and a space-indented recipe fails with a message that does not mention whitespace.
memories.content: Recipes must be tab-indented. A space-indented line produces a missing-separator error that names the line but not the cause. Editors that convert tabs on save cause this repeatedly.

memories.gist: Adding an environment to the config does not add it to CI, which runs an explicit list.
memories.content: CI enumerates environments explicitly rather than running the whole list, so a newly added environment is never executed and appears to pass. Add it in both places.

memories.gist: Migration 0039 is not reversible; its down step raises deliberately because the data cannot be reconstructed.
memories.content: 0039 collapses two columns into one and the original split cannot be recovered. The down step raises rather than pretending. A rollback past it therefore requires a restore, which is documented in the runbook.

memories.gist: Migration 0051 must run after the application deploy, not before, because it drops a column the old code still reads.
memories.content: Ordinary ordering is migrate-then-deploy. 0051 is the exception: it removes a column the previous release still selects, so running it first breaks the running version. Deploy, verify, then migrate.

memories.gist: The backfill in 0055 is chunked and resumable, but rerunning it from the start double-counts a derived column.
memories.content: It records progress in a checkpoint table and resumes from there. Starting it over without clearing the checkpoint reapplies increments to the derived column. Clear the checkpoint or resume, never restart blind.

memories.gist: The migration history was squashed at 0030, so a database older than that cannot be migrated forward directly.
memories.content: Everything before 0030 was collapsed into a baseline. An old database has history the runner does not recognise and refuses to proceed. Restore from a recent snapshot instead of migrating an ancient copy.

memories.gist: The health endpoint's own timeout is 5 seconds, which is shorter than the dependency check it performs.
memories.content: The check calls a dependency whose own timeout is longer than the health endpoint's, so under dependency slowness the health check times out rather than reporting unhealthy. The nested timeouts need ordering; currently they are inverted.

memories.gist: The client's default socket timeout is 60 seconds, which is longer than the gateway's, so the client never sees the gateway's rejection cleanly.
memories.content: Because the client waits longer than the gateway does, the gateway's termination arrives as a truncated response rather than a status. Set the client timeout below the gateway's so the failure is attributable.

memories.gist: The list endpoint silently caps the page size at 1000 regardless of what you ask for, and does not indicate truncation.
memories.content: Requesting more than the cap returns exactly the cap with no flag and no next-page token in some code paths, so a caller reading a large collection stops early believing it is done. Always follow pagination even when you asked for everything.

memories.gist: Message payloads above 64 kilobytes are rejected by the broker, and the producer's error is generic.
memories.content: The broker enforces a maximum message size. The producer surfaces it as a generic send failure without naming size, so it is usually diagnosed as a connectivity problem. Compress or externalise large payloads.

memories.gist: The bulk endpoint accepts up to 500 items per call and partially applies on failure, returning per-item status.
memories.content: A failing item does not roll back the others. The response carries per-item status which callers routinely ignore, so partial failures are invisible. Check every item's status, not just the HTTP code.

memories.gist: Negative lookups are cached for the same duration as positive ones, so a newly created record is invisible for five minutes.
memories.content: A miss is cached, so creating a record after something looked for it means the miss is served until it expires. This is the cause of the create-then-immediately-fetch failures. Invalidate on create, which the write path does not currently do.

memories.gist: There is no single-flight guard, so an expiring hot key produces a burst of identical upstream requests.
memories.content: When a hot key expires every concurrent request misses and calls upstream. The upstream sees a spike that looks like a traffic event. A single-flight wrapper is the standard fix and is not implemented.

memories.gist: Timestamps are serialised without an offset in one legacy endpoint, and consumers assume local time.
memories.content: One endpoint emits an offset-less timestamp. Consumers differ on how they interpret it and at least one assumes local time. New endpoints must always emit an offset. Changing the legacy one requires coordinating with two consumers.

memories.gist: Large integer ids lose precision when serialised for JavaScript consumers, so ids are emitted as strings.
memories.content: Ids exceed the safe integer range for double-precision consumers and silently round. They are therefore serialised as strings. A new endpoint that emits them as numbers reintroduces the bug for those consumers only.

memories.gist: The internal endpoint requires the server name extension, and one older client omits it, receiving the default certificate and failing verification.
memories.content: Without the extension the load balancer serves a default certificate that does not match the requested host, so verification fails. The error looks like a certificate mismatch on our side. The old client needs the host set explicitly.

memories.gist: Certificate pinning in the mobile client means a certificate rotation requires a client release first.
memories.content: The pin is on the leaf, so rotation breaks every un-upgraded client. Rotation therefore has to be staged behind a client release. Moving the pin to the intermediate is the accepted improvement, not yet done.

memories.gist: The test suite is not network isolated, so a test that accidentally hits a real endpoint passes locally and fails in the sandbox.
memories.content: There is no outbound block in the test environment, so an un-mocked call silently reaches the real service. In the isolated CI sandbox it fails, which is where such tests are usually discovered. Add the block locally too.

memories.gist: Snapshot tests regenerate silently when the update flag is left in a developer's shell profile, which is how a wrong snapshot got committed.
memories.content: With the update flag exported, a failing snapshot test rewrites the snapshot and passes. Someone had it in their profile permanently. Never export it; pass it per invocation.

memories.gist: Freezing time in a test leaks into other tests when the fixture is module-scoped, producing bizarre unrelated failures.
memories.content: The time freeze is applied at module scope in one file and, because the patch is global, tests in other files running afterwards in the same worker see the frozen clock. Scope it to the function.

memories.gist: The seed data includes one row with a deliberately null optional field, and several tests depend on that row's position.
memories.content: Ordering of seed rows is not guaranteed but a few tests index into the seeded set positionally. Adding a row at the start of the seed file breaks them in a way that looks unrelated. Reference seed rows by their natural key.

memories.gist: A small share of CI runs fail on name resolution for the package index; the retry wrapper covers the install step but not the tool bootstrap.
memories.content: Resolution failures happen in maybe one run in fifty. The install step retries, the bootstrap that fetches the tool itself does not, so that is where the failure surfaces. Wrapping the bootstrap is the outstanding fix.

memories.gist: Reproducible builds require the timestamp variable to be set; without it the artefact hash changes on every build.
memories.content: Embedded build timestamps make the output non-deterministic, which defeats the artefact cache. Set the standard timestamp variable from the commit date. It is set in CI and usually not locally, so local and CI hashes differ.

memories.gist: Build artefacts are retained for 14 days, so reproducing a failure from a month-old run requires rebuilding.
memories.content: Retention is two weeks. Older runs keep their logs but not their artefacts. If a failure matters, download the artefact while it exists.

memories.gist: Logs are retained for 7 days at full fidelity and 90 days sampled, so an investigation older than a week has gaps.
memories.content: Full logs age out after a week into a sampled tier. An investigation into something a month old will find partial evidence and it is easy to mistake sampling gaps for absence of events.

memories.gist: Deadlines are not propagated across one hop, so an inner call can outlive the outer request that no longer wants it.
memories.content: One service creates a fresh context instead of deriving from the incoming one, so the deadline is lost at that hop. Work continues after the caller has given up, which wastes capacity during an incident. Derive the context.

memories.gist: One proxy in the path does not multiplex, so a burst of parallel requests queues behind a single connection.
memories.content: Parallelism collapses at that hop because it serialises onto one upstream connection. Client-side concurrency above a small number therefore adds latency rather than throughput. The proxy replacement is planned.

memories.gist: The connection pool is sized smaller than the worker thread count, so threads block on pool checkout under load.
memories.content: With more workers than pool slots, checkout becomes the bottleneck and presents as database slowness even though the database is idle. Size the pool at or above the worker count, mindful of the server's own connection limit.

memories.gist: Transaction pooling breaks prepared statements and advisory session locks, which is why two features silently misbehave through the pooler.
memories.content: In transaction pooling mode a session is not stable across statements, so session-scoped state is lost. Prepared statements and session advisory locks are the two things we hit. Use a direct connection for those paths.

memories.gist: The most-updated table's indexes bloat and need periodic rebuilding, which the maintenance job does not currently cover.
memories.content: Heavy update churn leaves the indexes several times larger than necessary, which slowly degrades scans. The maintenance job vacuums but does not rebuild. A manual concurrent rebuild has been done twice by hand.

memories.gist: Running the analysing form of explain executes the statement, so it is not safe to use on a write statement in production.
memories.content: The analysing variant actually runs the query. On a write statement that means the write happens. Wrap it in a transaction you roll back, or use the plan-only form.

memories.gist: Queries against the JSON column cannot use a plain index and need an expression index per accessed path.
memories.content: There is no general index for arbitrary paths. Each frequently-filtered path needs its own expression index, and there are currently three, so a query on a fourth path is a full scan. Check before adding a filter on a new path.

memories.gist: Random primary keys fragment the index badly at this table's insert rate; the newer tables use time-ordered ids.
memories.content: Random ids scatter inserts across the index and cause heavy page splitting. Newer tables use a time-ordered identifier for this reason. Converting the existing table is a large migration nobody has scheduled.

memories.gist: The partial index excludes soft-deleted rows, so a query that does not filter on the active flag will not use it.
memories.content: The index carries a predicate on the active flag. Omitting that filter from the query makes the index unusable and the planner falls back to a scan. Always include the flag in the predicate, even when it seems redundant.

memories.gist: Promoting the replica is manual and the application does not re-resolve the endpoint, so a failover needs a restart too.
memories.content: Promotion changes which host is writable but the application caches the resolved address for the life of the process. A failover therefore requires a rolling restart to take effect. This is documented in the runbook and easy to forget.

memories.gist: A full restore takes about four hours, which is longer than the stated recovery objective; the gap is accepted and documented.
memories.content: Measured restore time on the production-sized dataset is roughly four hours end to end, against a stated objective of one. The gap is known and accepted rather than fixed. Do not promise the objective in a design review.

memories.gist: The audit table is append-only at the database level, so a test that cleans up after itself cannot delete its audit rows.
memories.content: A rule blocks deletes on the audit table. Tests that write audited actions leave rows behind permanently, which is intended. Use a separate database for tests rather than trying to clean up.

memories.gist: Request bodies must never be logged at debug level because they carry personal data; the redacting logger exists for this.
memories.content: Debug logging of raw bodies is a compliance problem, not merely untidy. The redacting wrapper is available and must be used for anything that can contain a body. A review caught this once already.

memories.gist: The rate limit is per credential, not per instance, so scaling out does not increase available throughput.
memories.content: The limit applies to the credential, so more instances share the same budget and each gets less. Scaling out to fix rate-limit errors makes them slightly worse by adding retry pressure. Request a higher limit instead.

memories.gist: Incoming webhooks can be replayed by the sender for up to 24 hours, so handlers must be idempotent on the event id.
memories.content: The sender retries for a day on any non-success, and also replays on their own operational events. Handlers must deduplicate on the event id, which two of ours do not.

memories.gist: Webhook signature verification must run on the raw body; any middleware that reparses and re-serialises breaks it.
memories.content: The signature covers the exact bytes. A body-parsing middleware that hands the handler a re-serialised body changes whitespace and key order and verification fails. Capture the raw body before parsing.

memories.gist: The preflight response is cached by browsers for ten minutes, so a header change appears not to take effect.
memories.content: Preflight results are cached client-side. After changing allowed headers, existing browser sessions keep the old answer for the cache duration. Test in a fresh profile before concluding the change did not work.

memories.gist: The load balancer keeps sending traffic for up to 30 seconds after an instance is marked unhealthy, so the drain wait must exceed that.
memories.content: Deregistration is not immediate. An instance that exits as soon as it is marked unhealthy drops in-flight requests. The shutdown must wait longer than the deregistration delay, which is currently not the case for one service.
